claim: The hair cell mechanotransduction (MET) channel complex is essential for hearing.
source: The hair cell mechanotransduction (MET) channel complex is essential for hearing, yet it's molecular identity and structure remain elusive.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the MET channel's role in hearing.

claim: The molecular identity and structure of the MET channel remain elusive.
source: The hair cell mechanotransduction (MET) channel complex is essential for hearing, yet it's molecular identity and structure remain elusive.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: TMC1 protein localizes to the site of the MET channel.
source: The transmembrane channel–like 1 (TMC1) protein localizes to the site of the MET channel, interacts with the tip-link responsible for mechanical gating, and genetic alterations in TMC1 alter MET channel properties and cause deafness, supporting the hypothesis that TMC1 forms the MET channel.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: A model of TMC1 was generated based on X-ray and cryo-EM structures of TMEM16 proteins.
source: We generated a model of TMC1 based on X-ray and cryo-EM structures of TMEM16 proteins, revealing the presence of a large cavity near the protein-lipid interface that also harbors the Beethoven mutation, suggesting that it could function as a permeation pathway.
evidence: This describes the methodology and results of the modeling work performed in this study.

claim: The TMC1 model reveals a large cavity near the protein-lipid interface.

claim: The Beethoven mutation is located in the large cavity near the protein-lipid interface in the TMC1 model.

claim: The large cavity in TMC1 could function as a permeation pathway.

claim: Hair cells are permeable to 3 kDa dextrans.
source: We also find that hair cells are permeable to 3 kDa dextrans, and that dextran permeation requires TMC1/2 proteins and functional MET channels, supporting the presence of a large permeation pathway and the hypothesis that TMC1 is a pore forming subunit of the MET channel complex.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the dextran uptake experiments.

claim: Dextran permeation requires TMC1/2 proteins.
source: We also find that hair cells are permeable to 3 kDa dextrans, and that dextran permeation requires TMC1/2 proteins and functional MET channels, supporting the presence of a large permeation pathway and the hypothesis that TMC1 is a pore forming subunit of the MET channel complex.

claim: Dextran permeation requires functional MET channels.
source: We also find that hair cells are permeable to 3 kDa dextrans, and that dextran permeation requires TMC1/2 proteins and functional MET channels, supporting the presence of a large permeation pathway and the hypothesis that TMC1 is a pore forming subunit of the MET channel complex.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the blocker and BAPTA experiments.

claim: The MET channel converts mechanical stimulus produced by sound waves into electrical signals.
source: The mechanotransduction (MET) channel in hair cells of the vertebrate inner ear convert the mechanical stimulus produced by sound waves into electrical signals that are transmitted into the central nervous system and is therefore essential for the perception of sound (Fettiplace and Kim, 2014; Gillespie and Müller, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The MET channel is essential for the perception of sound.
source: The mechanotransduction (MET) channel in hair cells of the vertebrate inner ear convert the mechanical stimulus produced by sound waves into electrical signals that are transmitted into the central nervous system and is therefore essential for the perception of sound (Fettiplace and Kim, 2014; Gillespie and Müller, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Hair cells are capable of detecting small and rapid displacements of the mechanosensitive stereocilia bundle.
source: Hair cells are highly specialized sensory cells capable of detecting small and rapid displacements of the mechanosensitive stereocilia bundle at the cell apex (Corey and Hudspeth, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The sensory stereocilia bundle consists of three rows of actin-based stereocilia arranged in a staircase fashion.
source: The sensory stereocilia bundle consists of three rows of actin-based stereocilia arranged in a staircase fashion and connected by an extracellular protein filament or tip link that is formed by protocadherin 15 (PCDH15) and cadherin 23, and that mechanically gates the MET channel (Ahmed et al., 2006; Fettiplace and Kim, 2014; Furness et al., 2008; Gillespie and Müller, 2009; Kachar et al., 2000; Kazmierczak et al., 2007; Sotomayor et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Stereocilia are connected by an extracellular protein filament called the tip link.
source: The sensory stereocilia bundle consists of three rows of actin-based stereocilia arranged in a staircase fashion and connected by an extracellular protein filament or tip link that is formed by protocadherin 15 (PCDH15) and cadherin 23, and that mechanically gates the MET channel (Ahmed et al., 2006; Fettiplace and Kim, 2014; Furness et al., 2008; Gillespie and Müller, 2009; Kachar et al., 2000; Kazmierczak et al., 2007; Sotomayor et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The tip link is formed by protocadherin 15 (PCDH15) and cadherin 23.

evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The tip link mechanically gates the MET channel.
source: The sensory stereocilia bundle consists of three rows of actin-based stereocilia arranged in a staircase fashion and connected by an extracellular protein filament or tip link that is formed by protocadherin 15 (PCDH15) and cadherin 23, and that mechanically gates the MET channel (Ahmed et al., 2006; Fettiplace and Kim, 2014; Furness et al., 2008; Gillespie and Müller, 2009; Kachar et al., 2000; Kazmierczak et al., 2007; Sotomayor et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The MET channel has a large conductance (150–300 pS in low Ca2+).
source: Electrophysiological studies of hair cells reveal that the MET channel is a large conductance (150–300 pS in low Ca2+) and cation-selective channel (Beurg et al., 2006; Corey and Hudspeth, 1979; GéléocGeleoc et al., 1997; Kros et al., 1992; Ohmori, 1985) that is permeable to relatively large organic compounds, including quaternary ammonium ions, FM1-43 and aminoglycoside antibiotics (Alharazneh et al., 2011; Gale et al., 2001; Marcotti et al., 2005; Meyers et al., 2003; Ohmori, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: The MET channel is cation-selective.
source: Electrophysiological studies of hair cells reveal that the MET channel is a large conductance (150–300 pS in low Ca2+) and cation-selective channel (Beurg et al., 2006; Corey and Hudspeth, 1979; GéléocGeleoc et al., 1997; Kros et al., 1992; Ohmori, 1985) that is permeable to relatively large organic compounds, including quaternary ammonium ions, FM1-43 and aminoglycoside antibiotics (Alharazneh et al., 2011; Gale et al., 2001; Marcotti et al., 2005; Meyers et al., 2003; Ohmori, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: The MET channel is permeable to quaternary ammonium ions, FM1-43 and aminoglycoside antibiotics.

evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: TMC1 is the most abundant subtype expressed in mature auditory hair cells.
source: TMC1 is the most abundant subtype expressed in mature auditory hair cells, whereas TMC2 is more abundantly expressed early in postnatal development, coinciding with the onset of mechanotransduction (Corns et al., 2017; Kawashima et al., 2011, 2015; Kim and Fettiplace, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous expression studies.

claim: TMC2 is more abundantly expressed early in postnatal development.
source: TMC1 is the most abundant subtype expressed in mature auditory hair cells, whereas TMC2 is more abundantly expressed early in postnatal development, coinciding with the onset of mechanotransduction (Corns et al., 2017; Kawashima et al., 2011, 2015; Kim and Fettiplace, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous expression studies.

claim: TMC2 expression coincides with the onset of mechanotransduction.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous expression studies.

claim: Hair cells from TMC1 and TMC2 double knockout mice appear structurally unperturbed at P5.
source: Hair cells from TMC1 and TMC2 double knockout mice appear structurally unperturbed at P5, yet exhibit no MET channel currents (Pan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Hair cells from TMC1 and TMC2 double knockout mice exhibit no MET channel currents.
source: Hair cells from TMC1 and TMC2 double knockout mice appear structurally unperturbed at P5, yet exhibit no MET channel currents (Pan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: TMC1 and TMC2 biochemically interact with the tip link.
source: Both TMC1 and TMC2 have been shown to biochemically interact with the tip link that is required for mechanical gating of the MET channel (Assad et al., 1991; Maeda et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TMC1 and TMC2 are expressed at the tip of the shorter stereocilia.
source: In addition, both TMC1 and TMC2 are expressed at the tip of the shorter stereocilia (Kurima et al., 2015) where the MET channel has been localized (Beurg et al., 2009).

claim: TMC proteins have been proposed to be related to TMEM16 proteins.
source: The TMC proteins have been proposed to be related to TMEM16 proteins (Hahn et al., 2009; Medrano-Soto et al., 2018), a fascinating family of membrane proteins that have been shown to function as Ca2+-activated Cl- channels (TMEM16A,B) (Dang et al., 2017; Hartzell and Whitlock, 2016; Paulino et al., 2017; Peters et al., 2018; Schroeder et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2008) or as Ca2+-activated lipid scramblases (e.g. TMEM16F) (Brunner et al., 2014; Malvezzi et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

source: The TMC proteins have been proposed to be related to TMEM16 proteins (Hahn et al., 2009; Medrano-Soto et al., 2018), a fascinating family of membrane proteins that have been shown to function as Ca2+-activated Cl- channels (TMEM16A,B) (Dang et al., 2017; Hartzell and Whitlock, 2016; Paulino et al., 2017; Peters et al., 2018; Schroeder et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2008) or as Ca2+-activated lipid scramblases (e.g. TMEM16F) (Brunner et al., 2014; Malvezzi et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2012).

source: Using this approach, nhTMEM16 (Brunner et al., 2014)(PDB ID: 4WIS) and mTMEM16A (Paulino et al., 2017)(PDB IDs: 5OYB and 5OYG) stand out as the best templates for TMC1 when compared to other candidates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: mTMC1 has 12% sequence identity with nhTMEM16.

claim: mTMC1 has 11% sequence identity with mTMEM16A.

evidence: This is based on the sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2A,B.

claim: The three TMC1 models displayed an overall similar architecture, consisting of 10 TM helices, two helices in the N-terminus, one helix in the C-terminus, three long extracellular loops and one long intracellular loop.
source: As expected, these three models displayed an overall similar architecture, consisting of 10 TM helices, two helices in the N-terminus, one helix in the C-terminus, three long extracellular loops (TM1-TM2, TM5-TM6 and TM9-TM10) and one long intracellular loop (TM2-TM3) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a description of the structural models shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The predicted transmembrane topology of TMC1 is distinct from earlier models containing between 6 and 8 TMs.
source: The predicted transmembrane topology of the TMC1 protein is distinct from earlier models containing between 6 and 8 TMs (Fettiplace, 2016; Holt et al., 2014; Kawashima et al., 2015; Labay et al., 2010), providing a revised framework to identify extracellular glycosylation sites and intracellular regulatory motifs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This compares the current model to previous models cited in the literature.

claim: The mTMC1 models were generated as dimers.
source: Our TMC1 models were generated as dimers, similar to the templates used, with a two-fold symmetry axis located between the two TM10 helices (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Residues in TM10 forming the dimer interface are highly conserved.
source: Residues in TM10 forming the dimer interface are highly conserved, consistent with TMC1 forming dimers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the conservation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each TMC1 protomer contains a cavity formed by helices TM4-TM7 that faces the membrane.
source: Each protomer contained a cavity formed by helices TM4-TM7 that faces the membrane.
evidence: This is a description of the structural models.

claim: The major divergences among the three TMC1 models were dictated by the structural templates, which exhibited unique rearrangements of helices TM4 and TM6.
source: The major divergences among the three models were dictated by the structural templates, which exhibited unique rearrangements of helices TM4 and TM6 that contour the cavity (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an analysis of the differences between models shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The cavity observed in model 1 was wide open, forming a deep cleft towards the lipid bilayer.
source: The cavity observed in model 1 was wide open, forming a deep cleft towards the lipid bilayer, whereas in model 2, the cavity was narrower at the extracellular side and partially shielded from the membrane.
evidence: This is a description of the structural features of model 1.

claim: In model 2, the cavity was narrower at the extracellular side and partially shielded from the membrane.
source: The cavity observed in model 1 was wide open, forming a deep cleft towards the lipid bilayer, whereas in model 2, the cavity was narrower at the extracellular side and partially shielded from the membrane.
evidence: This is a description of the structural features of model 2.

claim: In model 3, the intracellular end of the TM6 helix bends over the cavity to further diminish the exposure of the cavity to the surrounding membrane.
source: In model 3, the intracellular end of the TM6 helix bends over the cavity to further diminish the exposure of the cavity to the surrounding membrane.
evidence: This is a description of the structural features of model 3.

claim: The global ProQM score of model 1 was 0.612, higher than the scores of model 2 (0.577) and model 3 (0.564).
source: The global ProQM score of model 1 was 0.612, higher than the scores of model 2 (0.577) and model 3 (0.564).
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of model quality.

claim: The local ProQM scores of residues located in TM4-6 were higher in model 1 compared to model 2 and model 3.
source: We found that the local ProQM scores of residues located in TM4-6 were higher in model 1 compared to model 2 and model 3 (Figure 2C), indicating that TMC1 is more likely to contain a deep cavity, similar to that observed in the nhTMEM16 structure.
evidence: This is based on the local ProQM analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TMC1 is more likely to contain a deep cavity, similar to that observed in the nhTMEM16 structure.
source: We found that the local ProQM scores of residues located in TM4-6 were higher in model 1 compared to model 2 and model 3 (Figure 2C), indicating that TMC1 is more likely to contain a deep cavity, similar to that observed in the nhTMEM16 structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the local ProQM analysis.

claim: Four helices in TMC1 model 1 contribute to forming the cavity that faces the membrane environment.
source: Four helices in TMC1 model 1 contribute to forming the cavity that faces the membrane environment, with the more hydrophobic TM5 and TM7 helices located deep within the cavity, and TM4 and TM6 helices located more peripherally.
evidence: This is a description of the structural features of model 1.

claim: TM4 and TM6 contain many polar residues, including seven acidic residues, two basic residues and nine uncharged polar residues.
source: TM4 and TM6 contain many polar residues, including seven acidic residues, two basic residues and nine uncharged polar residues, giving the cavity considerable hydrophilic character (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on the analysis of residues shown in Figure 3C.

claim: TMC1 lacks the six acidic residues located behind the cavity in TMEM16 proteins that coordinate Ca2+ and are required for activation.
source: Interestingly, TMC1 lacks the six acidic residues located behind the cavity in TMEM16 proteins that coordinate Ca2+ and are required for activation (Brunner et al., 2014; Tien et al., 2014)(Figure 1C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is based on comparison with TMEM16 structures and supported by citations.

claim: The surface of the cavity in TMC1 model 1 exhibits a negative electrostatic potential.
source: The surface of the cavity in TMC1 model 1 exhibits a negative electrostatic potential (Figure 3D), consistent with the cation selectivity observed for the MET channel (Corey and Hudspeth, 1979).
evidence: This is based on electrostatic potential calculations shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Residues lining the cavity in TMC1 model 1 show strong sequence conservation among TMC proteins.
source: Importantly, residues lining the cavity in TMC1 model 1 show strong sequence conservation among TMC proteins (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the cavity is a conserved feature of these proteins.
evidence: This is based on the conservation analysis shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cavity is a conserved feature of TMC proteins.
source: Importantly, residues lining the cavity in TMC1 model 1 show strong sequence conservation among TMC proteins (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the cavity is a conserved feature of these proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation analysis.

claim: The TMC domain (residues 512–631 in mTMC1) is the most highly conserved region among TMC homologs.
source: Indeed, the TMC domain (residues 512–631 in mTMC1, NP_083229.1) is the most highly conserved region among TMC homologs (Kawashima et al., 2015; Kurima et al., 2003) and this domain is formed by the TM6-TM8 helices, all of which contribute to forming the cavity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The TMC domain is formed by the TM6-TM8 helices, all of which contribute to forming the cavity.
source: Indeed, the TMC domain (residues 512–631 in mTMC1, NP_083229.1) is the most highly conserved region among TMC homologs (Kawashima et al., 2015; Kurima et al., 2003) and this domain is formed by the TM6-TM8 helices, all of which contribute to forming the cavity.
evidence: This is based on the structural model and domain analysis.

claim: Out of thirty missense deafness-causing TMC1 mutations identified to date, twenty human and two mouse mutations are within regions modeled.
source: Out of the thirty missense deafness-causing TMC1 mutations identified to date, twenty human and two mouse mutations are within regions we modeled (Figure 4 and Figure 4—source data 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the analysis of mutations shown in Figure 4 and related figures.

claim: Nine deafness-causing mutations are found in TM4 and TM5.
source: Interestingly, nine of these mutations are found in TM4 and TM5, two of the helices that form the cavity.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of mutation locations in the model.

claim: Two positions where mutations cause autosomal dominant deafness are found in the cavity, including the M412K Beethoven mutant and D569N/H.
source: In particular, two positions where mutations cause autosomal dominant deafness are found in the cavity, including the M412K Bth mutant (M418K in hTMC1) and D569N/H (D572N/H in hTMC1) (Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the analysis of mutation locations shown in Figure 4 and related figures.

claim: When organ of Corti explants from wild-type postnatal day (P) 6 mice were incubated for 2 hr with dextran-TR at room temperature, robust and specific labeling of auditory hair cells was observed.
source: When organ of Corti explants from wild-type postnatal day (P) 6 mice were incubated for 2 hr with dextran-TR at room temperature, we observed robust and specific labeling of auditory hair cells using confocal Airyscan super-resolution microscopy (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 5.

claim: Labeling was observed for both inner and outer hair cells along the entire organ of Corti from the basal to the apical regions.
source: Labeling was observed for both the inner and outer hair cells (IHC and OHC) along the entire organ of Corti from the basal to the apical regions (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: Hair cells from the basal area incorporated significantly more dextran compared to those from the middle or the apical regions.
source: Interestingly, we found that hair cells from the basal area incorporated significantly more dextran compared to those from the middle or the apical regions (Figure 5C,D), a result that is consistent with reports for uptake of FM1-43 (Gale et al., 2001; Lelli et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 5C,D and supported by citations.

claim: Only hair cells that incorporated dextran-TR in their cell body also showed fluorescent labeling of their stereocilia.
source: When we imaged both stereocilia and cell bodies, we observed that only those cells that incorporated dextran-TR in their cell body also showed fluorescent labeling of their stereocilia (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Hair cells whose stereocilia displayed the strongest signals also had the strongest fluorescence signals in their cell bodies.
